title: Water and sanitation access is expanding while stress, inequality, data gaps, and local financing constrain service security
source_unit: United Nations Statistics Division, Sustainable Development Goals Report 2026, Goal 6: Clean Water and Sanitation
geography: Global comparison of drinking water, sanitation, hygiene, water stress, quality monitoring, and water-governance systems

observations.period: 2015-2024; drinking water, sanitation, and hygiene coverage

denominator.unit: global population and household service coverage

safely_managed_drinking_water_2024.unit: percent of the world's population with safely managed drinking water in 2024

safely_managed_sanitation_2024.unit: percent of the world's population with safely managed sanitation in 2024

basic_hygiene_2024.unit: percent of the world's population with basic hygiene services in 2024

gains_since_2015.value: 961 million people gained safely managed drinking water, 1.2 billion gained safely managed sanitation, and 1.6 billion gained basic hygiene services between 2015 and 2024

observations.method: UN SDG compilation of household water, sanitation, and hygiene coverage indicators.
observations.uncertainty: Coverage definitions, reporting quality, service continuity, affordability, and within-country inequality affect comparability; access does not establish safety at every moment or equal household control.
observations.subgroup: Urban and rural populations, least developed countries, low-income countries, conflict-affected populations, women, children, and households lacking safely managed services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Aggregate coverage gains can represent meaningful improvements in health, time, dignity, and security even when service quality, affordability, and conflict-related interruptions remain unresolved.

observations.period: 2024; inequality by development and stability context

denominator.unit: global service-coverage comparison across country-development and conflict contexts

ldc_service_gap.value: people in least developed countries were roughly two to three times more likely to lack essential water, sanitation, and hygiene services than the global average

conflict_service_gap.value: countries affected by conflict and instability lagged stable countries by 33 to 38 percentage points across the three service measures

rural_drinking_water.unit: percent safely managed drinking-water coverage in rural areas in 2024

rural_sanitation.unit: percent safely managed sanitation coverage in rural areas in 2024

observations.method: UN SDG disaggregation of water, sanitation, and hygiene access by rurality, country development status, and conflict or stability context.
observations.uncertainty: Relative gaps combine different country groups and may reflect infrastructure, conflict, income, geography, reporting, and institutional factors; they do not identify a single causal mechanism.
observations.subgroup: Least developed countries, conflict-affected populations, rural households, children, women and girls, and communities with weak service infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rural gains show that targeted infrastructure and service expansion can work, but local maintenance, climate shocks, affordability, and political stability determine durability.

denominator.unit: global water-use efficiency and freshwater stress indicators

water_use_efficiency_growth.unit: percent improvement in global water-use efficiency between 2015 and 2023

water_use_efficiency_2023.unit: US dollars of economic output per cubic metre of water in 2023

high_or_critical_stress_population.unit: percent of global population living in countries with high or critical water stress

global_average_water_stress.unit: percent global average water stress in 2023

observations.method: UN SDG synthesis of water-use efficiency, freshwater withdrawal, and water-stress indicators.
observations.uncertainty: Water-use efficiency can rise through economic growth without reducing withdrawals or improving ecosystem conditions; national averages hide seasonal, basin-level, and household stress.
observations.subgroup: Water-stressed regions, agriculture, industry, cities, households, ecosystems, and communities dependent on shared or declining freshwater sources.
observations.counterinterpretation: Efficiency improvements can create room for development and adaptation, but rebound effects, allocation choices, and unequal access can offset system-level gains.

denominator.unit: countries surveyed for integrated water-resources management and governance conditions

water_quality_reporting_2023.unit: countries reporting water-quality data in 2023, up from 72 in 2017

integrated_water_management_score.unit: global average score out of 100 for integrated water-resources management in 2023

countries_significantly_behind.unit: countries significantly behind in implementing water-management frameworks

countries_insufficient_revenue.unit: percent of countries reporting insufficient revenue to implement water-management plans

local_basin_funding_gap.unit: approximate percent of countries lacking adequate funding at local and basin levels

observations.method: UN SDG review of water-quality monitoring, integrated water-resources management, transboundary cooperation, community participation, and financing.
observations.uncertainty: Reporting counts and governance scores measure formal capacity and self-reported conditions, not service reliability or pollution reduction; financing gaps vary by basin and institutional level.
observations.subgroup: Water agencies, local and basin authorities, transboundary communities, citizen scientists, Indigenous and local communities, and households dependent on public or shared water systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Expanded monitoring and cooperation can strengthen accountability and conflict prevention even before service outcomes improve; citizen data can partly close official information gaps.

related_sources.claim: UN-Water World Water Development Report 2026 provides complementary gendered-time and water-governance evidence.
UN SDG 14 provides complementary marine and coastal water-system evidence.

boundary: This record adds a global water-service and governance route linking drinking water, sanitation, hygiene, rural and conflict inequality, water stress, monitoring, basin cooperation, community participation, and finance. It uses aggregate SDG indicators and country-level governance reporting, not individual health outcomes, household service histories, causal infrastructure estimates, or proof that formal plans deliver reliable services.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UN SDG 2026 Goal 6 page was reviewed for global coverage, gains since 2015, rural and conflict gaps, water-use efficiency, stress, water-quality reporting, integrated management, participation, cooperation, and financing figures.
